tier_reason: The checked-in paper 'Large Scale Learning to Rank' (D. Sculley) has Table 1 with RCV1 E311 CPU training seconds (SVM-struct-rank 30,716.33 s, SVM-perf-roc 31.92 s, SPD Pass-Aggr .22 s, SPD SGD-SVM .20 s, SPD Pegasos .20 s) and the LETOR text (0.2-0.3 CPU s, up to 100x vs SVM-light, up to 5x vs SVM-struct-rank), all first-party; the author's 2009-12-09 commit calls it a NIPS workshop paper, but no CPU model, compiler, flags or benchmark scripts are given, so C.

corrections.caveats: First-party numbers by the author (D. Sculley, Google) in the paper 'Large Scale Learning to Rank' checked into the repo (papers/stochastic-rank.pdf). The PDF prints no venue; the author's commit of 2009-12-09 ('Adding NIPS workshop paper on fast learning to rank') identifies it as a NIPS 2009 workshop paper, whose review process could not be checked here, so it is treated as first-party (tier C). Hardware is a dual-core 2.8GHz laptop with 2G RAM, no CPU model; compiler and flags are not stated and the repo ships no benchmark scripts. The timing covers 100,000 SGD steps of an approximate stochastic pairwise learner against exact RankSVM solvers (SVM-light, SVM-struct-rank, SVM-perf-roc) trained to the same ROC area, so the speedup comes from an algorithm change, not faster code for the same algorithm. On LETOR the RankSVM accuracy comparison uses previously published LETOR results, and the paper does not say whether the SVM-light and SVM-struct-rank training times were rerun on the same laptop. The README's 10x (reference Pegasos) and 3x (svm_perf) data-reading claims give no method, and its 0.1 CPU s figure for 100,000 Pegasos steps on RCV1 CCAT is from a different (2.4GHz) laptop. Not compared with liblinear, Vowpal Wabbit, TensorFlow or PyTorch. The original code.google.com/p/sofia-ml page was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so this record uses glycerine's GitHub import (described on GitHub as 'Automatically exported from code.google.com/p/sofia-ml'); the last commit 2016-02-13 is the import itself, and the author's last code commit is dated 2010-07-26 ('Adding combined-ranking and combined-roc, and logistic prediction option').

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the paper (Table 1 and the LETOR Training Speed paragraph; 'more than 150 times faster' than SVM-perf-roc is the paper's own phrase, 160x is derived). Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0 (COPYING is the Apache License 2.0 text), 63 stars, 20 forks, not a fork, not archived, abandoned. Shortcomings: first-party workshop paper, no CPU model, compiler or flags, algorithmic speedup of an approximate SGD learner vs exact solvers, README parse-speed claims without method.

tier_reason: SciMLBenchmarks (independent third-party suite; source benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd in SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl) shows SymEngine beating SymPy on every workload, with CPU (AMD EPYC 7502), Julia 1.13.0 and LLVM 20.1.8 stated; libsymengine is the prebuilt SymEngine_jll 0.12.0+0 whose Yggdrasil recipe gives CMake options but no build type or compiler version, and the SymPy version is unpinned, so not A.

corrections.workload: Ten summary workloads run as SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 (libsymengine from SymEngine_jll 0.12.0+0) against SymPy (timed inside Python with time.perf_counter, called via PythonCall.jl) and SymbolicUtils.jl: some adapted from symengine's own C++ benchmark suite (derivative of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50), 15-term series of sin(cos(1+x)), substitution into a trig product, numeric evaluation of a 10000-deep expression, lambda code generation and compiled-call time) and some taken from SymbolicUtils' own suite (substitution into a random expression with 10^5 draws, variable search on common-subtree and dissimilar expressions); plus a separate expand((x+y+z+w)^n) table for n = 8 to 32. Minimum of samples; SymPy caches cleared before each sample.
corrections.claimed_speedup: SymEngine vs SymPy, seconds from the page's summary table (ratios derived from page data): diff of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50) 0.00696 vs 6.98 (about 1000x); series 15 terms 0.00199 vs 1.43 (about 720x); substitute trig product 1.48e-5 vs 6.57e-3 (about 440x); substitute 10^5-draw random expression, dense rule 0.00113 vs 2.30 (about 2000x) and sparse rule 0.00110 vs 1.07 (about 970x); variable search 0.00103 vs 0.0149 (about 15x) and on dissimilar expressions 0.000467 vs 0.00508 (about 11x); eval_double of a 10000-deep expression 0.0117 vs 31.06 (about 2660x); codegen init 0.00115 vs 0.0514 (about 45x); compiled call with CSE 6.93e-7 vs 8.41e-6 (about 12x). The expand((x+y+z+w)^32) table gives 0.0153 s vs 3.46 s (about 226x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13.0 (LLVM 20.1.8); libsymengine from SymEngine_jll v0.12.0+0, a BinaryBuilder binary whose public Yggdrasil recipe (S/SymEngine/build_tarballs.jl) passes BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=yes, WITH_MPC=yes and WITH_SYMENGINE_THREAD_SAFE=yes with GMP/MPFR/MPC dependencies but no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or compiler version; SymPy installed unpinned through pip via CondaPkg (benchmarks/Symbolics/CondaPkg.toml), version not shown
corrections.caveats: The page is an independent benchmark by SciML maintainers (Aayush Sabharwal, Chris Rackauckas; SciMLBenchmarks.jl file benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd, code public, CPU stated), but they also maintain SymbolicUtils.jl, and the first workload set was adapted from SymEngine's own suite and is described on the page as playing to a compiled symbolic kernel. The same page shows SymEngine losing to pure-Julia SymbolicUtils.jl on sparse-rule substitution (0.00110 s vs 0.000593 s), variable search (0.00103 s vs 0.00049 s with IRStructure), the compiled call with CSE (6.93e-7 s vs 3.13e-7 s) and the compiled call without CSE (1.07e-5 s vs 2.56e-6 s). The random-expression substitution compares unequal trees: realized node counts are 3271 for SymEngine, 2810 for SymbolicUtils and 8498 for SymPy, so the 2000x and 970x ratios overstate the per-node gap. The eval_double row pits SymEngine's native C++ evalf against a hand-written Python bottom-up evaluator built on SymPy constructors (SymPy's own evalf is exponential in nesting depth here), timed as a single call of about 31 s rather than a minimum of samples. SymEngine is reached through the SymEngine.jl ccall wrapper; SymPy is pure Python, so a compiled-versus-interpreted gap is expected. Build type and compiler of the prebuilt libsymengine 0.12.0 (not the newest release) and the SymPy version are not stated, hence B rather than A; the benchmark file is a single recent run. SymEngine's own repo has no README or wiki claim with SymPy numbers: the wiki pages found earlier (Optimizing expand2b, Univariate Series expansion benchmarks) only compare SymEngine variants and Piranha. Older comparisons with GiNaC, Sage and CSymPy sit in blocked pages. The wave 8 categories have no symbolic-algebra bucket; big-integer-arbitrary-precision was chosen to sit beside FLINT (SymEngine uses GMP/FLINT/MPFR/MPC for exact and arbitrary-precision coefficients).

notes: All ten summary ratios check out against the page's HTML tables (derived ratios correct to rounding). baseline_in_list corrected to false: SymPy is not among wave 8 baselines (big-integer-arbitrary-precision lists GMP and MPFR). Repo checked on github.com: MIT, 1.4k stars, 314 forks, last commit 2026-09-04, active. Category: no spec Part 4 category covers symbolic algebra; big-integer-arbitrary-precision is the least-bad wave 8 fit (exact arithmetic on GMP/FLINT), otherwise a new symbolic-algebra category would be needed. Shortcomings to record: unequal random trees in the substitution rows (8498 SymPy nodes vs 3271), eval_double against a hand-written Python evaluator, losses to SymbolicUtils.jl on four rows, unpinned SymPy and unstated build type/compiler of the prebuilt libsymengine.

tier_reason: benchmark_url is null and the only source, the gamedev.net forum thread 'Efficiency : Bullet much slower than PhysX?', is EGRESS_BLOCKED; the numbers survive only as WebSearch snippets, and the repo README has no performance text, so per the null-benchmark rule the record cannot stay above D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only, unverified (gamedev.net forum post, page blocked): capsule sweeps onto a triangle-mesh terrain, 1 capsule 0.132 ms (PhysX) vs 0.757 ms (Bullet); 100 capsules 3.790 ms (PhysX) vs 73.388 ms (Bullet); the poster summarises Bullet as costing about 10 times more (ratios about 5.7x and 19.4x, derived from the snippet numbers).
corrections.caveats: Evidence is WebSearch snippets only. The source is a gamedev.net forum thread, 'Efficiency : Bullet much slower than PhysX?' (https://www.gamedev.net/forums/topic/600114-efficiency-bullet-much-slower-than-physx/), which was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the date, PhysX and Bullet versions, hardware, compiler and flags are unknown; the thread is probably old and likely predates the PhysX 3.4 code in this repo. A search summary of the same thread also mentions 500 capsules at 488 ms (Bullet) vs 43 ms (PhysX) and a reply questioning the setup (whether hardware acceleration was on in both engines, and whether Bullet's btHeightfieldTerrainShape should have been used instead of a triangle-mesh shape); snippet only, unverified. It is one user's forum anecdote of sweep (raycast-style) queries on a mesh, not rigid-body stepping. The peer-reviewed Erez, Tassa and Todorov ICRA 2015 comparison of Bullet, Havok, MuJoCo, ODE and PhysX exists (homes.cs.washington.edu PDF, blocked here; no GitHub copy found); its search summary says no engine wins overall and gaming engines do best on gaming-style tests, so it was not used for a speedup claim. Pierre Terdiman's PEEL ships no results, the Gazebo benchmark does not include PhysX, and the PhysX-3.4 README has no performance text. Bullet is not among the geometry-spatial baselines (Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS, R-trees), and a physics engine fits that category only loosely through its collision queries. The repo is the 2018 PhysX 3.4 snapshot (last commit 2018-12-05, BSD-3-Clause per README); newer PhysX releases live elsewhere and were not opened.

notes: Downgraded C to D: no openable benchmark page; the forum thread is blocked and its numbers come from search snippets, with a reply in the same thread questioning the Bullet setup. Not rejected: PhysX is notable (2.4k stars on this repo, 297 forks, widely embedded). Metadata checked on github.com: BSD-3-Clause license text in README, not archived, last commit 2018-12-05, abandoned. If kept, record shortcomings: forum anecdote only, versions/hardware unknown, possible Bullet misuse (triangle mesh instead of heightfield), off-baseline for geometry-spatial.
